title: The Rechabites: A Lesson in Faithfulness
summary: In the reign of Jehoiakim, the LORD tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabite family into a temple chamber and set wine before them. They refuse, explaining that their ancestor Jonadab commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow fields, or plant vineyards, but to live in tents, and they have kept his command for generations. God holds up their loyalty to a human ancestor as a rebuke to Judah, which will not obey its God, and promises the Rechabites that their line will always have a man to stand before him.
story: The chapter steps back in time from the siege of Zedekiah's reign (chapter 34) to the days of Jehoiakim, about a decade earlier. The book is arranged here by theme rather than date. Chapter 34 showed Judah making a solemn promise and breaking it within weeks; chapter 35 shows a small clan keeping a promise for over two centuries. The two chapters together frame the question that runs through the book: will God's people listen? The Rechabites become a living parable, and the chapter's closing promise to them is one of the few words of blessing in this part of Jeremiah. Chapter 36 continues in Jehoiakim's reign, with the king burning Jeremiah's scroll.
historical:
Verse 11 explains why these tent dwellers were in Jerusalem: they had fled there when Nebuchadnezzar's armies, including Chaldean and Aramean troops, came into the land. That fits the last years of Jehoiakim, around 599 to 598 BC, when 2 Kings 24:1-2 says that after Jehoiakim rebelled against Babylon, the LORD sent raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Judah.

The Rechabites' ancestor Jonadab (or Jehonadab) son of Rechab appears in 2 Kings 10:15-27 as an ally of Jehu, the army commander who seized the northern throne around 841 BC and violently purged the worship of Baal. So the family's rule was roughly two and a half centuries old by Jeremiah's day. 1 Chronicles 2:55 connects the house of Rechab with the Kenites, a clan related to Moses' in-laws who lived among Israel, though the details of that genealogy are obscure. The temple officials named in verse 4, such as Maaseiah the doorkeeper, were among the officers who guarded the temple gates and managed its rooms.
cultural:
Most Judeans lived in villages and towns, farmed grain, and tended vineyards; wine was an ordinary part of meals and feasts. The Rechabites deliberately refused that settled life. They lived in tents, did not own fields or vineyards, and drank no wine. The reasons are not stated. Many scholars think Jonadab meant to keep his family close to the simpler life of Israel's wilderness years and apart from the farming culture of Canaan that was tied up with the worship of Baal, which would fit his zeal against Baal in 2 Kings 10. Their vow resembles the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, which also forbade wine, but it was a permanent family rule rather than a personal and temporary one.

The temple complex had side rooms around its courts used for storage, for priests and Levites, and for meetings. Hanan son of Igdaliah is called a man of God, a title often used for a prophet, so the room may have belonged to a group of prophets or their disciples. Setting pitchers of wine before the Rechabites in the temple, in public, made the test as strong as it could be.
literary: The chapter is a prophetic sign-act built around a contrast. Verses 1 to 11 tell the story: the command, the scene in the temple chamber, and the Rechabites' refusal, told at length in their own words. Verses 12 to 17 apply it to Judah by an argument from the lesser to the greater: if a family obeys a human ancestor who spoke once, how much more should a nation obey the God who has spoken again and again. The word obey (shama, to hear) runs through the whole chapter. Verses 18 and 19 turn to the Rechabites with a blessing. God did not intend for Jeremiah to tempt them into disobedience; he knew they would refuse, and their refusal was the message.

outline.t: Wine set before the Rechabites in the temple
Their refusal and the command of Jonadab
The lesson for Judah: they obey, you do not
A promise to the house of Rechab

doctrines.note: The Rechabites show faithfulness over generations: a costly way of life kept not because it was easy but because it had been commanded. God points to such steady loyalty as the shape obedience to him should take.
God's complaint is not that Judah never heard, but that he spoke “again and again” through the prophets calling them to turn (verses 14-15). Persistent refusal to listen is the heart of their guilt.
A father's command shaped his family for centuries. The chapter shows the power of what one generation hands to the next, for good or ill.

words.note: Shama, to hear, and in this sense to obey. In Hebrew, to hear someone's voice often means to do what they say. The Rechabites have heard their ancestor's voice (verse 8), while Judah has not heard the LORD (verse 16). Listening and obeying are one act.

Mitsvah, commandment. Used here of Jonadab's commands (verses 14 and 18), it is the same word used for God's commandments in the law. The comparison is pointed: a man's commandment is kept, God's is not.

Ohel, tent. Tents recalled Israel's wilderness years and the patriarchs, who lived as sojourners in the land. The Rechabites' tents were a lifelong sign that they did not treat the land as a settled possession.

Rechabite, a member of the house of Rechab. As a group the Rechabites are known almost only from this chapter; their ancestor appears in 2 Kings 10, and the house of Rechab is named in 1 Chronicles 2:55. The name marks them as a family defined by one ancestor and his word.

christ: The chapter's argument from the lesser to the greater reappears in the New Testament. Hebrews 12:9 reasons that we respected our earthly fathers who disciplined us, and asks whether we should not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live. Jesus' parable of the two sons, one who says he will obey and does not and one who refuses and then obeys (Matthew 21:28-32), makes a similar point to Judah's leaders about hearing and doing. Above all, the New Testament presents Jesus as the one who perfectly heard and obeyed his Father, doing nothing on his own but only what he saw the Father doing (John 5:19), and learning obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). These are thematic connections; the New Testament does not mention the Rechabites.

hard.q: Is God endorsing abstinence from wine, or saying that all family traditions should be kept?
hard.a: No on both counts, if the chapter is read on its own terms. God does not command Judah to live like the Rechabites; he commends the Rechabites for their faithfulness to the rule they had received. Scripture elsewhere treats wine both as God's good gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15) and as dangerous when abused (Proverbs 20:1). Christians have differed on whether abstinence is wise, and this passage does not settle that question. Nor is the lesson that every inherited custom must be kept; some traditions ought to be abandoned, and Jesus rebuked people who set aside God's command for the sake of their tradition (Mark 7:8-9). The point is the contrast: a human family kept a human word faithfully, while God's people ignored God's word. Jonadab's rule was a demanding but harmless one, and the Rechabites' loyalty to it shamed a nation that had broken far more important commands.

questions: The Rechabites kept their ancestor's command for over two centuries. What convictions are you passing on to those who come after you, and how?
God argued that if people can be faithful to a human father, they should be faithful to him. Where do you find it easier to keep a human commitment than a commitment to God?
The Rechabites lived in tents as a sign that they were not settled. What might it look like to hold your possessions and home with an open hand?
